name: NYISO
desc: Positions engaging the New York ISO (NYISO) specifically.

letters.desc: National Grid highlights NYISO's existing large load interconnection procedures as a model the Commission should allow regions to build upon. The NYISO cluster study cycle is approximately 567 days; a 20 MW threshold would overwhelm that process with small projects that could connect faster outside it.
quotes: A final rule should reflect this reality and be limited to truly large loads as defined on a region-by-region basis, which in most regions, including New York and New England, is likely to be at a higher MW threshold than 20 MW.

National Grid is concerned that a bright line 20 MW test for defining "large loads" will not be workable in many regions of the nation.  Such a low threshold could subject smaller projects with minimal reliability impact or required upgrades to a cluster study process or other large load interconnection process in the NYISO and ISO-NE regions that extends for a long time.

The NYISO already has procedures in place to study large loads interconnecting to the transmission system.  Allowing the NYISO and other regions to leverage these existing processes will help avoid unnecessary delays and support innovation.

letters.org: New York State Public Service Commission
letters.desc: The NYSPSC points to NYISO tariff provisions and the NYSPSC's own T&D utility oversight as evidence that New York already has adequate processes to evaluate large load interconnections for reliability and resource adequacy impacts, without federal intervention.
quotes: the NYSPSC has significant concerns with the scope of the Proposed ANOPR, which would intrude on matters reserved to the states under the Federal Power Act (FPA), namely service to end-use/retail customers.
New York already has the necessary procedures in place to make sure these interconnections do not compromise reliability or resource adequacy.

current interconnection processes in New York require large loads to pay for the cost of their interconnection and related transmission upgrades, the operation of large loads may impose other costs not reflected in the interconnection process.

these large loads will require significant amounts of generation and their appearance on the electric grid will add to the need for more generation to meet statewide electric demand needs and thereby raise the costs for all customers.
Given the NYPSC's regulatory oversight of the T&D utilities, the NYPSC is in the best position to identify these costs and allocate them appropriately.

letters.org: Utility Intervention Unit, New York State Department of Stat
letters.desc: The UIU asks FERC to build large-load rules on NYISO's Attachment HH and Manual 23 processes, which already address load modeling, queue administration, and cost allocation. Overriding them risks confusion and relitigating settled cost-allocation precedents.
quotes: Any new large load rules should be built upon NYISO's established interconnection processes, manuals, and datasets rather than overriding them.

Creating a national standard could introduce confusion, conflicting study timelines, or inconsistent cost-responsibility determinations at a time when speed in the interconnection process is needed most.

letters.org: New York Independent System Operator, Inc.
letters.desc: NYISO describes its own shrinking generation reserve margins, driven by retirements outpacing new supply, as context for why large load growth in New York raises particular reliability concerns that a uniform national rule may not adequately address.
quotes: the current fleet of generating resources connected to the New York Control Area ("NYCA") is decreasing while insufficient generation with the necessary characteristics is entering service.

letters.desc: The NYTOs describe New York's layered federal-regional-state reliability framework in detail, including NYISO's TEI Manual study thresholds, NYSRC and NPCC coordination, and ongoing 2026 stakeholder priority projects on large-load integration. They present these processes as evidence that cooperative federalism already works and should be reinforced, not supplanted.
quotes: building on NYISO's existing Commission-approved reliability planning processes that coordinate these comprehensive mechanisms—rather than creating an entirely new structure for transmission-level load—will promote continuity and make use of experience already gained.

letters.desc: TBA cites NYISO's 2026 initiative to develop flexible load models as confirmation that formal study constructs are needed and that RTOs are moving in this direction.
quotes: NYISO also identifies the development of "Flexible Load models for Large Loads" as a priority in its ongoing internal work plan—a clear recognition that formal modeling constructs are needed to appropriately study and integrate flexible load
